title: Blood Meridian; or, The Evening Redness in the West

mechanics.premise: A nameless teenager joins the Glanton gang of scalp hunters across the U.S.-Mexico borderlands (c. 1849-1850); the novel follows escalating atrocity and the ascent of the antagonist Judge Holden.
mechanics.point_of_view: Third person, middle-to-far psychic distance; the prose records violence as world-fact rather than as narratorial outrage.
mechanics.style_and_devices: Spare parataxis, biblical cadence, concrete noun-heavy catalogues, minimal evaluative adjectives, and withheld moral commentary; landscape treated as a sublime, indifferent force.
mechanics.emotional_progression: Appetite for violence -> normalized atrocity -> metaphysical dread -> implied judgement that the reader must supply.
mechanics.dialogue: Terse, aphoristic exchanges; the antagonist's oratory supplies philosophic justification that the narration never endorses.
mechanics.setting: Arid borderlands, desert, and burning settlements rendered as indifferent space.
mechanics.critical_reception: Initially lukewarm, later recognised as McCarthy's magnum opus and a central American novel; cited here for style, not for any reproduced passage.
mechanics.verification_note: Existence, date, publisher, and premise confirmed via Wikipedia 'Blood Meridian' and the Wikipedia API extract; stylistic reading attributed to Vereen Bell (1988) and general critical consensus. No text reproduced.
